questions.stem: A worker stands near a sealed gamma source for 10 minutes but does not touch it. After the source is removed, is the worker still exposed to radiation?

options.text: Yes, because the gamma rays remain in the worker's body
Yes, because the worker has become radioactive
No, because the worker was only irradiated -- once the source is removed, exposure stops
No, because gamma rays cannot affect humans

questions.explanation: This is irradiation, not contamination. The worker was exposed to radiation from an external source. Once the source is removed, the exposure stops immediately. The worker does not become radioactive (B) -- irradiation does not make objects radioactive. Gamma rays do not 'remain' in the body (A). Gamma rays can certainly affect humans (D) -- they can damage cells and DNA.

questions.stem: Which situation represents contamination rather than irradiation?

options.text: A patient having a chest X-ray at a hospital
A worker standing 2 metres from a sealed radioactive source
Radioactive dust settling on a worker's skin after a nuclear accident
A person walking past a cabinet containing radioactive materials

questions.explanation: Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or into a person's body. Radioactive dust on the skin (C) is contamination -- the radioactive material is in direct contact with the person and continues to irradiate them until removed. Options A, B, and D are all examples of irradiation -- exposure to radiation from an external source at a distance. Contamination is generally more dangerous because the source cannot simply be 'removed' by walking away.

questions.stem: A scientist handles a radioactive source in a laboratory. Which precaution reduces their exposure using the principle of distance?

options.text: Wearing a lead apron
Using long-handled tongs to hold the source
Storing the source in a lead-lined container
Limiting the time spent near the source

questions.explanation: The three key principles for reducing radiation exposure are: time, distance, and shielding. Using long-handled tongs increases the distance between the source and the scientist's body, reducing the radiation dose received. Wearing a lead apron (A) and using a lead-lined container (C) are examples of shielding. Limiting time spent near the source (D) is the time principle. All are valid precautions, but only B addresses the distance principle.

questions.stem: Alpha radiation is considered the most dangerous type of radiation if a source is ingested (swallowed). Why?

options.text: Alpha particles travel the furthest inside the body, damaging many organs
Alpha particles are strongly ionising and deposit all their energy in a small area of tissue, causing concentrated damage to cells
Alpha particles cannot be detected by medical equipment
Alpha particles are the only type of radiation that can damage DNA

questions.explanation: Alpha particles are the most ionising type of radiation. When inside the body, their high ionising power means they deposit all their energy in a very small volume of tissue, causing intense, concentrated damage to cells and DNA. Their short range (A is wrong -- they travel the shortest distance) actually makes them MORE dangerous internally, because all the energy is absorbed locally. All types of radiation can damage DNA (D is wrong), but alpha causes the most damage per particle due to its high ionisation.

questions.stem: A nuclear power plant worker receives a radiation dose of 2 mSv per month. The annual dose limit is 20 mSv. After how many months would the worker reach the annual limit?

options.text: 5 months
10 months
12 months
20 months

questions.explanation: Annual limit / monthly dose = 20 mSv / 2 mSv per month = 10 months. After 10 months, the worker would have accumulated 20 mSv, reaching the annual limit. This means the worker would need to be reassigned to duties with lower radiation exposure for the remaining 2 months of the year, or the monthly dose must be reduced. This demonstrates why monitoring cumulative exposure is essential for radiation workers.
